blocks.title: Exercises on maps, quotients, and duality
blocks.tex: These optional problems connect the chapter's different descriptions of linear maps. The first problems use definitions and basis constructions; the later ones ask for factorization arguments and precise control of ranks. No exercise depends on another exercise.

blocks.title: Conjugation and the scalar field
blocks.tex: Define $C:\C\to\C$ by $C(x+iy)=x-iy$ for real $x,y$. Prove that $C$ is a linear isomorphism when both copies of $\C$ are real vector spaces, but is not linear when their scalar field is $\C$.
blocks.proof: For $z=x+iy$ and $w=u+iv$, direct addition gives $C(z+w)=(x+u)-i(y+v)=Cz+Cw$. If $a\in\R$, $C(az)=ax-iay=aCz$. Thus $C$ is real-linear. Applying $C$ twice restores both coordinates, so $CC=I$, and $C$ is its own inverse. Over complex scalars, $C(i\cdot1)=-i$ whereas $iC(1)=i$. Since $i\ne-i$, complex homogeneity fails.
hints: Compare real and complex homogeneity separately.

blocks.title: Agreement on a spanning list
blocks.tex: Let $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ span $V$, and let $S,T\in\Lin(V,W)$. Prove that $S=T$ if $Sv_j=Tv_j$ for every $j$. Does the list have to be independent?
blocks.proof: For $v\in V$, choose coefficients with $v=\sum_ja_jv_j$. Linearity gives $Sv=\sum_ja_jSv_j=\sum_ja_jTv_j=Tv$. Thus the maps agree at every input. If $n=0$, the domain is zero and both maps take its only vector to zero, giving the same conclusion. Independence was never needed: existence of an expansion suffices, regardless of how many expansions are possible.
hints: Apply both maps to any one spanning expansion of a vector.

blocks.title: Prescribing both kernel and range
blocks.tex: Let $V$ be finite-dimensional, let $U\subseteq V$ be a subspace, and let $R$ be a finite-dimensional subspace of a vector space $W$. Prove that a map $T\in\Lin(V,W)$ with $\Null T=U$ and $\Range T=R$ exists exactly when $\dim U+\dim R=\dim V$.
blocks.proof: If such a map exists, rank-nullity gives the asserted equality. Conversely, choose a basis $u_1,\ldots,u_k$ of $U$ and extend it to a basis $u_1,\ldots,u_k,v_1,\ldots,v_r$ of $V$. The dimension equality gives $r=\dim R$; choose a basis $w_1,\ldots,w_r$ of $R$. The basis prescription theorem defines a linear map by $Tu_i=0$ and $Tv_j=w_j$. For the unique expansion $x=\sum a_iu_i+\sum b_jv_j$, its image is $\sum b_jw_j$. This image is zero exactly when every $b_j=0$, by independence of the $w$ basis. That is exactly the condition $x\in U$. Its possible images are all combinations of the $w$ basis, exactly $R$. Empty lists give the same proof when $U=V$ or $R=\{0\}$.
hints: Necessity is a dimension count.
For sufficiency, extend a basis of the desired kernel and prescribe the images of the added vectors.

blocks.title: Translation as a polynomial isomorphism
blocks.tex: For $a\in\F$ and $n\ge0$, define $T_a:\Poly_n(\F)\to\Poly_n(\F)$ by $(T_ap)(z)=p(z+a)$. Prove that $T_a$ is a linear isomorphism with inverse $T_{-a}$.
blocks.proof: For $p(z)=\sum_{j=0}^nc_jz^j$, expanding each product $(z+a)^j$ by distributivity gives powers of $z$ of degree at most $j$, so $p(z+a)$ has degree at most $n$, or is zero. Thus $T_a$ has the asserted target. At each $z$, $(T_a(p+q))(z)=p(z+a)+q(z+a)$ and $(T_a(cp))(z)=cp(z+a)$, proving linearity. Composing substitutions gives $(T_{-a}T_ap)(z)=p((z-a)+a)=p(z)$ and $(T_aT_{-a}p)(z)=p((z+a)-a)=p(z)$. Both maps preserve the bounded-degree space by the same expansion argument, so they are two-sided inverses there.
hints: Check the degree bound before composing translations.

blocks.title: Combining two maps records an intersection
blocks.tex: If $S\in\Lin(V,W)$ and $T\in\Lin(V,Z)$, define $A:V\to W\times Z$ by $Av=(Sv,Tv)$. Prove that $A$ is linear and $\Null A=\Null S\cap\Null T$. If $V,W,Z$ are finite-dimensional, deduce $\dim(\Null S\cap\Null T)\ge\dim V-\dim W-\dim Z$.
blocks.proof:
The product operations give $A(u+v)=(Su+Sv,Tu+Tv)=Au+Av$ and $A(av)=(aSv,aTv)=aAv$. Its output is the zero pair exactly when both $Sv=0$ and $Tv=0$, proving the kernel identity. In the finite-dimensional case, rank-nullity and the dimension bound for subspaces give
\[\dim\Null A=\dim V-\dim\Range A\ge\dim V-\dim(W\times Z)=\dim V-\dim W-\dim Z.\]
Substitute the kernel identity. The inequality remains valid when its right side is negative.
hints: Use the product space as target of a single map.

blocks.title: Dimension of the image of a subspace
blocks.tex:
Let $T\in\Lin(V,W)$ and let $U\subseteq V$ be a finite-dimensional subspace. Write $T(U)=\{Tu:u\in U\}$. Prove that $T(U)$ is a finite-dimensional subspace of $W$ and
\[\dim T(U)=\dim U-\dim(U\cap\Null T).\]
blocks.proof: Restrict $T$ to inputs in $U$, obtaining $T|_U:U\to W$. Its linearity follows from the same identities as for $T$, because operations on $U$ are inherited. Its range is $T(U)$ by definition, so the range-subspace theorem makes this a subspace. Its kernel consists precisely of vectors that belong to $U$ and satisfy $Tu=0$, hence is $U\cap\Null T$. Applying rank-nullity to the finite-dimensional domain $U$ gives finite-dimensionality of the range and the displayed formula.
hints: Apply rank-nullity to the restriction of the map to $U$.

blocks.title: Upper and lower bounds for the rank of a composition
blocks.tex:
Let $V,W,Z$ be finite-dimensional and $T\in\Lin(V,W)$, $S\in\Lin(W,Z)$. Set $r(T)=\dim\Range T$, and similarly for the other maps. Prove
\[r(S)+r(T)-\dim W\le r(ST)\le\min(r(S),r(T)).\]
blocks.proof:
Consider the restriction $A=S|_{\Range T}:\Range T\to Z$, which is linear because $\Range T$ is a subspace. Its range equals $\Range(ST)$: outputs in either set have the form $S(Tv)$. Its kernel is $\Range T\cap\Null S$. Rank-nullity gives
\[r(ST)=r(T)-\dim(\Range T\cap\Null S).\]
The intersection is a subspace of $\Null S$, so its dimension is at most $\dim\Null S=\dim W-r(S)$. Substitution gives the lower bound. Its dimension is nonnegative, giving $r(ST)\le r(T)$. Finally $\Range(ST)\subseteq\Range S$, so the subspace dimension inequality gives $r(ST)\le r(S)$. Together these prove both bounds, including all zero-dimensional cases.
hints: Restrict the outer map to the range of the inner map.
Identify the kernel of that restriction.

blocks.title: A right inverse characterizes surjectivity
blocks.tex: Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional and $T\in\Lin(V,W)$. Prove that $T$ is surjective if and only if there exists $R\in\Lin(W,V)$ such that $TR=I_W$.
blocks.proof: If $TR=I_W$, then every $w\in W$ equals $T(Rw)$, so $T$ is surjective. Conversely, choose a basis $w_1,\ldots,w_m$ of $W$. Surjectivity supplies $v_j\in V$ with $Tv_j=w_j$. Prescribe $Rw_j=v_j$ and extend linearly using the basis prescription theorem. For $w=\sum a_jw_j$, linearity gives $TRw=\sum a_jTv_j=\sum a_jw_j=w$. Thus $TR=I_W$. If $W=\{0\}$, the basis is empty and its unique linear map to $V$ is zero; its composition with $T$ is the identity on the zero space.
hints: Choose preimages for a basis of the target.

blocks.title: A left inverse characterizes injectivity
blocks.tex: Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional and $T\in\Lin(V,W)$. Prove that $T$ is injective if and only if there exists $L\in\Lin(W,V)$ such that $LT=I_V$.
blocks.proof: If $LT=I_V$ and $Tu=Tv$, applying $L$ gives $u=v$, so $T$ is injective. Conversely choose a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $V$. The list $Tv_1,\ldots,Tv_n$ is independent: a relation $\sum a_jTv_j=0$ gives $T(\sum a_jv_j)=0$, injectivity implies $\sum a_jv_j=0$, and independence gives every $a_j=0$. Extend this image list to a basis of $W$. Define $L$ on this basis by $L(Tv_j)=v_j$ and by sending every added basis vector to zero; extend linearly. For each basis vector of $V$, $LTv_j=v_j$, and linear expansion then gives $LTv=v$ for every $v$. If $V=\{0\}$, the image list is empty, this construction gives the zero map $L$, and the identity on $V$ is also zero.
hints: Extend the images of a basis of the domain to a basis of the target.

blocks.title: Maps that equal their own square
blocks.tex: Let $P\in\Lin(V)$ satisfy $P^2=P$, where $P^2=PP$. Prove that $V=\Null P\oplus\Range P$ and that $P$ acts as identity on its range. Conversely, for a decomposition $V=U\oplus W$, prove that the map sending $u+w$ to $w$ is linear, has square equal to itself, has null space $U$, and has range $W$.
blocks.proof:
If $w=Pv$, then $Pw=P^2v=Pv=w$, proving the assertion on the range. Each $v$ has the expression $v=(v-Pv)+Pv$, whose first term is in the null space because $P(v-Pv)=Pv-P^2v=0$, and whose second term is in the range. Thus the two subspaces sum to $V$. If $x$ lies in both, then $Px=0$ by its null-space membership and $Px=x$ by its range membership; hence $x=0$. The two-subspace directness criterion gives the decomposition.
Conversely directness gives a unique expression $v=u+w$, so the prescribed map is well-defined. Addition of two such expressions adds their $U$ parts and their $W$ parts, and scaling scales those two parts. Uniqueness therefore gives additivity and homogeneity of the map. A vector $w\in W$ has expression $0+w$ and is fixed. Thus the map has range $W$ and its square equals itself. An expression $u+w$ maps to zero exactly when $w=0$, which is equivalent to membership in $U$.
hints: For the first direction, decompose $v$ as $(v-Pv)+Pv$.

blocks.title: When a linear map descends to a quotient
blocks.tex: Let $U\subseteq V$ be a subspace and $T\in\Lin(V,W)$. Prove that a linear map $A:V/U\to W$ satisfying $A\pi=T$, where $\pi(v)=v+U$, exists exactly when $U\subseteq\Null T$. Prove that such $A$ is unique.
blocks.proof: If $A\pi=T$ and $u\in U$, then $\pi(u)=0+U$, the quotient zero. Hence $Tu=A(0+U)=0$ by linearity of $A$, proving $U\subseteq\Null T$. Conversely assume this inclusion and prescribe $A(v+U)=Tv$. If $v+U=w+U$, the coset equality criterion gives $v-w\in U\subseteq\Null T$. Thus $Tv-Tw=T(v-w)=0$ and the value is independent of the representative. The quotient operations and linearity of $T$ give $A((v+U)+(w+U))=T(v+w)=Tv+Tw$ and $A(a(v+U))=T(av)=aTv$, proving linearity. Its defining formula gives $A\pi=T$. If another map $B$ has this factorization, then for every coset $v+U$, $B(v+U)=B\pi(v)=Tv=A(v+U)$. Hence the map is unique. No finite-dimensionality is needed.
hints: Try the only possible formula, and determine when it is independent of the representative.

blocks.title: The annihilator of an intersection
blocks.tex:
For subspaces $U,W$ of a finite-dimensional space $V$, prove
\[(U\cap W)^0=U^0+W^0,\]
where $A^0=\{\varphi\in\dual{V}:\varphi|_A=0\}$.
blocks.proof:
If $\varphi\in U^0$ and $\psi\in W^0$, then for $x\in U\cap W$ both values vanish, so $(\varphi+\psi)(x)=0$. This gives $U^0+W^0\subseteq(U\cap W)^0$. Also $U^0\cap W^0=(U+W)^0$: vanishing on both $U$ and $W$ implies vanishing on every sum by additivity, while vanishing on $U+W$ implies vanishing on each subspace, which is contained in the sum. Put $n=\dim V$. The annihilator dimension theorem and the dimension formula for sums yield
\[\begin{aligned}
\dim(U^0+W^0)&=(n-\dim U)+(n-\dim W)-(n-\dim(U+W))\\
&=n-\dim(U\cap W)=\dim (U\cap W)^0.
\end{aligned}\]
All these spaces are finite-dimensional subspaces of $\dual{V}$. The earlier inclusion and equality of dimensions therefore imply equality of spaces.
hints: Prove one inclusion directly.
Identify $U^0\cap W^0$ and compare dimensions.

blocks.title: Evaluation identifies a finite-dimensional space with its double dual
blocks.tex: For finite-dimensional $V$, define $J:V\to\dual{(\dual{V})}$ by $(Jv)(\varphi)=\varphi(v)$. Prove that $J$ is a linear isomorphism.
blocks.proof:
For fixed $v$, pointwise operations on functionals give $(Jv)(a\varphi+b\psi)=a\varphi(v)+b\psi(v)$, so $Jv$ is a linear functional on $\dual{V}$; thus the target is correct. For $u,v\in V$ and scalars $a,b$, every $\varphi\in\dual{V}$ satisfies $(J(au+bv))(\varphi)=a\varphi(u)+b\varphi(v)$. Equality of functionals therefore gives $J(au+bv)=aJu+bJv$, proving linearity.
Choose a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ and its dual basis $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_n$. If $Jv=0$ and $v=\sum a_jv_j$, evaluating $Jv$ at $\varphi_k$ gives $0=\varphi_k(v)=a_k$. Hence $v=0$ and $J$ is injective. Applying the dual dimension theorem twice gives $\dim\dual{(\dual{V})}=\dim\dual{V}=\dim V$. The equal-dimension invertibility theorem now gives that $J$ is an isomorphism. For the zero space the basis and coordinate tests are empty; injectivity still follows because its only vector is zero.
hints: First check that $Jv$ is a functional.
Use the coordinate functionals of a basis to test whether $Jv=0$.

blocks.title: Duality preserves inverses
blocks.tex: If $T:V\to W$ is an invertible linear map, prove that $\dual{T}:\dual{W}\to\dual{V}$ is invertible and $(\dual{T})^{-1}=\dual{(T^{-1})}$. No finite-dimensionality is assumed.
blocks.proof:
The inverse $T^{-1}:W\to V$ is linear, so its dual has domain $\dual{V}$ and target $\dual{W}$. The reversal rule for duals of compositions gives
\[\dual{T}\,\dual{(T^{-1})}=\dual{(T^{-1}T)}=\dual{I_V}=I_{\dual{V}},\]
and
\[\dual{(T^{-1})}\,\dual{T}=\dual{(TT^{-1})}=\dual{I_W}=I_{\dual{W}}.\]
Here the identity-dual formula follows directly: for any functional $\varphi$, $\dual I(\varphi)=\varphi\circ I=\varphi$. Thus the two dual maps are two-sided inverses. Uniqueness of an inverse proves the stated formula.
hints: Dualizing a product reverses its order.

blocks.title: Equal kernels differ by an invertible change of target
blocks.tex: Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional and let $S,T\in\Lin(V,W)$. Prove that $\Null S=\Null T$ if and only if there is an invertible $A\in\Lin(W)$ with $S=AT$.
blocks.proof:
If $S=AT$ with $A$ invertible, injectivity of $A$ shows $Sv=0$ exactly when $Tv=0$, so the kernels agree. Conversely assume they agree. Define $B:\Range T\to\Range S$ by $B(Tv)=Sv$. If $Tv=Tw$, then $v-w\in\Null T=\Null S$, so $Sv=Sw$; hence $B$ is well-defined. For $Tv,Tw$ and scalars $a,b$, its definition and linearity of the original maps give $B(aTv+bTw)=S(av+bw)=aSv+bSw$, proving linearity. Every $Sv$ is an output of $B$, so it is surjective. If $B(Tv)=0$, then $v\in\Null S=\Null T$, giving $Tv=0$ and proving injectivity.
Choose a basis $y_1,\ldots,y_r$ of $\Range T$. Its images $By_1,\ldots,By_r$ form a basis of $\Range S$: they span by surjectivity and are independent by injectivity and linearity. Extend the first list to a basis $y_1,\ldots,y_r,u_1,\ldots,u_k$ of $W$ and the second to a basis $By_1,\ldots,By_r,w_1,\ldots,w_k$ of $W$. Their added lengths agree because both bases have length $\dim W$. Define $A$ to take the first basis to the second, entry by entry. This map has a linear inverse obtained by the reverse basis prescription, so it is invertible. It agrees with $B$ on $\Range T$, and therefore $ATv=B(Tv)=Sv$ for every $v$. If the common rank is zero, both image bases are empty and the same extension construction applies.
hints: First define an isomorphism only between the two ranges.
Equal kernels make the rule $Tv\mapsto Sv$ well-defined.
Extend compatible bases of the ranges to bases of the target.

blocks.title: Every feasible rank of a composition occurs
blocks.tex:
Let $a,b,c,r,s,t$ be nonnegative integers with $r\le\min(a,b)$ and $s\le\min(b,c)$. Prove that maps $T:\F^a\to\F^b$ and $S:\F^b\to\F^c$ with ranks $r,s$ and with $ST$ of rank $t$ exist exactly when
\[\max(0,r+s-b)\le t\le\min(r,s).\]
Here the rank of a map is the dimension of its range.
blocks.proof:
Suppose such maps exist. Restrict $S$ to $\Range T$. Its range is $\Range(ST)$ and its kernel is $\Range T\cap\Null S$, so rank-nullity gives $t=r-\dim(\Range T\cap\Null S)$. The intersection has dimension at most $\dim\Null S=b-s$ and at least zero. Thus $t\ge r+s-b$ and $t\le r$. Because $\Range(ST)\subseteq\Range S$, also $t\le s$; as a dimension, $t\ge0$. This proves necessity without relying on any other exercise.
Conversely assume the inequalities. Write the standard bases of the three coordinate spaces as $e_1,\ldots,e_a$, $f_1,\ldots,f_b$, and $g_1,\ldots,g_c$. Prescribe $Te_j=f_j$ for $j\le r$ and $Te_j=0$ for $j>r$. The basis prescription theorem supplies a linear map with range $\Span(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$, of dimension $r$.
Define $S$ on the middle basis by
\[Sf_j=\begin{cases}
g_j,&1\le j\le t,\\
g_{t+k},&j=r+k,\ 1\le k\le s-t,\\
0,&\text{all remaining indices}.
\end{cases}\]
The first two cases have disjoint index ranges because $t\le r$. The second uses available middle indices since $r+s-t\le b$, and all target indices are available since $s\le c$. Thus this is a valid basis prescription. Its nonzero images are exactly $g_1,\ldots,g_s$, so its range has dimension $s$. Of the vectors $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ produced by $T$, only $f_1,\ldots,f_t$ have nonzero images under $S$, and these images are $g_1,\ldots,g_t$. Consequently $ST$ has range of dimension $t$. Any interval of indices with zero intended length contributes no vectors, so the construction also covers every zero-dimensional or zero-rank case.
hints: Necessity follows by restricting $S$ to the range of $T$.
For sufficiency, let $T$ map onto the first $r$ coordinate directions.
Arrange that exactly $t$ of those directions survive $S$, and obtain the remaining rank of $S$ outside that range.
